A Black-owned web design company with one name behind it

If you searched for Black owned web developers, you probably want two things at once: someone you would be glad to send your money to, and a website that actually works for your business. This page is about both. Dominion Web Design Pro is a d/b/a of Dominion Digital Group, and it is owned by Maurice Johnson, a Black business owner in Big Sandy, Texas. He is not a front for a larger shop. He talks with you, writes your pages by hand and builds the site himself.

The business is small on purpose. There is no sales team passing you to an offshore production line, and no account manager who has never opened your site. When you want to know why a sentence on your About page reads the way it does, the person who wrote it is the person you ask.

Below you will find how we work, what we charge, and something most pages like this skip: how to check whether any company that calls itself Black-owned really is, and what to ask before you hire anyone at all.

What working with Maurice looks like

It starts with a free demo. You give your business name and what you do, and you get a preview site you can open on your phone, pass to your spouse or your business partner, and think about for a few days. There is no deposit and no call you have to sit through first.

If you like where it is going, Maurice asks the questions a stranger with a template never would. Who are your best customers? Which jobs do you want more of? What do people get wrong about your trade? What part of town do you actually drive to? Those answers become the pages. Every page on a finished site is written for that business and the towns it serves, never filled into a template from a list of city names.

You read every word before launch and change anything that does not sound like you. Then the site goes live, and you own it outright.

How to verify a business is Black-owned

"Black-owned" can mean a lot of things in a listing. Here is what each kind of evidence actually tells you.

What you seeWho decides itWhat it tells you
The company's own about pageThe businessA claim in its own words. Stronger when a named owner stands behind it and you can reach that person.
Google's Black-owned attribute on Maps, Search or ShoppingThe business opts inSelf-identification. Google lets the owner turn it on or off; it is not an ownership audit.
Listing in a Black-owned business directoryThe directory's own rulesVaries widely. Some directories review applications, many simply accept a form.
MBE certification from NMSDC or a regional councilThe certifying council, after a reviewThe firm showed it is at least 51% owned, operated and controlled by minority U.S. citizens.
State or city minority or historically underutilized business programsThat governmentThe firm met that program's rules, which differ from one state or city to the next.

For most small business owners hiring a web designer, the first row is the one that matters, as long as it is honest and specific. For a buyer at a company or agency with a supplier diversity goal, only the formal certifications usually count.

What MBE certification is, and what it is not

The National Minority Supplier Development Council (NMSDC) runs one of the best-known programs. Its definition of a minority business enterprise is a for-profit business that is at least 51% owned, operated and controlled by minority group members, and NMSDC lists Asian-Indian, Asian-Pacific, Black, Hispanic and Native American individuals as the groups it recognizes. The owners must be U.S. citizens and must be active in running the company day to day, not owners on paper only. The council checks this through documents, interviews and a site visit before it lists a firm.

That review is why large buyers rely on it. A corporation tracking how much it spends with minority suppliers needs more than a self-reported badge. NMSDC is also clear that certification opens doors to buyers; it does not promise any contracts.

Owner-claimed and formally reviewed are two different statements, and an honest company keeps them apart. Dominion Web Design Pro is Black-owned. It does not hold an MBE certification, an NMSDC listing or any state or city minority business certification, and nothing on this site says otherwise. If your purchasing department needs a certification number for its records, ask for it in writing from any vendor and look the number up with the council that issued it.

Why spending with Black-owned businesses still matters

Black-owned companies are a real and growing part of the economy, and they are still underrepresented among businesses large enough to hire staff. The U.S. Census Bureau's Annual Business Survey counted about 201,000 Black or African American-owned employer businesses in reference year 2023, with $249.0 billion in receipts. That was 3.4% of the roughly 5.9 million employer firms in the country, while the Census Bureau's population estimates put people who identify as Black alone at about 13.5% of Americans.

Most Black-owned businesses are one-person operations. The same Census release counted about 4.4 million Black or African American-owned nonemployer businesses in 2023, firms with no paid employees, with $128.7 billion in receipts. A lot of growing companies start right there: one owner, one truck or one chair, and a phone that needs to ring more often.

Access to money is part of why the gap persists. The Federal Reserve Banks' 2021 Small Business Credit Survey report on firms owned by people of color, based on a survey fielded in the fall of 2020, found that in the prior 12 months 13% of Black-owned firms that applied for non-emergency financing received all of it, compared with 40% of white-owned firms. When outside credit is harder to get, a business has to grow on the customers it can win, which is exactly the job a website is supposed to do.

None of that makes a site better or worse because of who built it. It is a reason some owners choose where their money goes, and that is their call to make.

Black owned web developers who know who reads your site

A barbershop on a busy corner, a home health agency, a cleaning crew, a church bookstore, a tax preparer who works out of a strip center every spring: the person reading the website is a customer deciding whether to call. They want to know what you do, where you work, what it costs or how to get a quote, and how fast you can get to them.

That is what Maurice writes toward. Service pages that say plainly what each service includes. A page for each town you actually serve. Hours, a map and a phone number on every page. A contact form that sends each lead to your email. Search basics done properly: page titles, descriptions, a sitemap submitted to Google, and on the Pro package, schema markup and Google Business Profile setup.

Whether or not being Black-owned is part of your own brand, your site should say what you want it to say. Some owners put it front and center; others leave it to the about page. That choice is yours, and Maurice writes it the way you want it.

Questions to ask any web developer before you sign

These apply to every Black owned web design agency, every freelancer and every large firm, including us. A good developer will answer all of them without hesitating.

  • What is the total price, in dollars, in writing? Including what renews monthly or yearly, and what happens if you stop paying it.
  • Who will register the domain, and in whose name? ICANN's registrant rules put the registered name holder in charge of the domain and its contact details. That should be you or your company, not the designer.
  • Who writes the pages? Hand-written for your business, or copied from a template and swapped for your name.
  • Can I see my site before I pay in full? A demo, a mockup or at least a draft you can open on your phone.
  • Who will I talk to after launch? A named person, or a ticket queue.
  • What will you not promise? Anyone who promises a ranking position or a set number of leads is guessing. Nobody controls Google.
  • If you claim a certification, which body issued it? Then look it up with that body.

Our own answers: the prices below, a site you own outright, every page written by hand by Maurice, a free demo before any money changes hands, and Maurice on the other end after launch. We do not promise rankings or lead counts. The longer version of this checklist is in our guide on how to hire a web designer.

Common questions

Are there Black owned web designers near me?

Possibly, and a search with your town name is a good start. But a website does not require a designer in your zip code. Maurice Johnson works from Big Sandy in East Texas and builds for small businesses across the country by phone, email and a shared preview link. If meeting in person matters to you, ask any designer you are considering where they actually work before you sign.

How can I tell if a web design company is really Black-owned?

Start with what the company says about who owns it and who does the work, and whether a named person stands behind it. Google's Black-owned attribute is chosen by the business itself, and many directory badges work the same way. Certification programs such as NMSDC's MBE certification are the formal route: they review ownership, control and citizenship before listing a firm. If a company claims a certification, ask for the certifying body and look it up there.

Does Dominion Web Design Pro have a minority business certification?

No. Dominion Web Design Pro, a d/b/a of Dominion Digital Group, is Black-owned: Maurice Johnson owns it and builds the sites. It does not hold an MBE, NMSDC, state or city minority business certification, and this page does not claim one. If your purchasing rules require a certification number, we are not the right fit for that contract.

How much do Black owned web developers charge for a small business website?

Prices vary by developer the same way they do across the whole industry, so ask each one for a written price in dollars. Ours are one time: Starter $497 for a 5-page site, Pro $997 for 10 pages plus 10 city pages, Agency $1,997 for a page for every town-and-service combination the keyword research supports. Hosting and maintenance are $49 a month, or included while you keep the AI agent.

What brands and businesses are Black-owned, and where can I find them?

There is no single official list. Useful places to look are the supplier directories run by certification councils such as NMSDC and its regional affiliates, the Black-owned attribute some businesses add to their Google Business Profile and Google Shopping listings, local Black chambers of commerce, and the business's own about page. Treat a badge as a starting point and the owner's own words as the better evidence.
